opus-5.5.text:
I think my teachers' reactions made a lot of sense, even when they seemed contradictory at first. Some of them were quite strict. They'd say, "If you use AI for this assignment, it counts as cheating," and I understood why. A lot of homework exists to make you struggle through something yourself. If you write an essay, the point isn't really the finished essay sitting on the teacher's desk, it's the process of organizing your thoughts and figuring out what you actually believe. If a model does that for you, you've skipped the part that was supposed to change you.

Other teachers were more open. They'd say, "Go ahead and use it, but tell me how you used it," or they'd redesign the assignment so that using AI was part of it, like asking us to critique what the model produced or to find where it was wrong. I found those assignments really interesting, because you had to know the material well enough to catch the mistakes, and that's sometimes harder than just writing it yourself.

So the way I see it, the teachers weren't really reacting to the technology itself. They were protecting the learning goal. When AI threatened that goal, they pushed back. When they could see a way to build it into the learning, they welcomed it. What made things a bit confusing for students was that every teacher drew the line in a different place, and the rules changed quickly because everyone, including the teachers, was still figuring it out.

Honestly, I sympathize with them. They had to change how they taught almost overnight, without much guidance, while students were often more familiar with the tools than they were. And as a student, I eventually came to realize the real question isn't "Am I allowed to use AI?" but "Am I still learning anything if I do?" When I'm honest with myself about that, the answer usually tells me what to do, whatever the rule happens to be.

r001.rationale: The response explains teachers’ reactions as protecting learning goals and adapting rules, but does not say they responded because they could not control whether students used AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think most of my teachers are in a kind of quiet panic, but they express it very differently.

There's roughly three types. The first type just bans it outright. They say if we catch you using AI, it's academic dishonesty, full stop. But everyone knows they can't actually catch it, so the rule becomes a bit theatrical. It turns into a game of who hides it better, not who learns more.

The second type pretends nothing has changed. They give the same homework they gave five years ago, the same essay prompts, and they grade them the same way. I actually find this the most frustrating, because the assignments were designed for a world where producing the text was the hard part. Now producing the text takes thirty seconds, so the assignment measures nothing. And I think deep down they know it.

The third type, which is still a minority, actually sat down and asked what the homework was for in the first place. One of my teachers switched to in-class writing and oral defense. You submit something, and then she asks you questions about it, face to face. If you used AI to write it, that's fine, but you'd better understand every sentence. I learned more in that class than in any of the ones with a ban.

What I've come to understand is that their reactions aren't really about AI. They're about trust and about time. Teachers don't have the time to redesign everything, and they've lost the ability to trust that a piece of paper reflects a student's thinking. So the ban is a way of buying time, and the pretending is a way of avoiding grief.

I don't blame them. But I do think the students who are honest with themselves can see which teachers are still asking the real question, which is: what do you actually know now that you didn't know before? The tool doesn't change that question at all. It just makes it impossible to fake the answer in the old ways.

r001.rationale: The response says teachers know they cannot reliably catch AI use, making outright bans theatrical and turning enforcement into a game of hiding it better. It connects their reactions to that lack of control.

astra-6.text: I think teachers are trying to figure out whether AI is helping us learn or just helping us finish the homework. If we hand in an answer we don’t understand, their concern makes sense. But using AI to explain something confusing or give feedback on our own work can be useful. So I’d understand a cautious response, though I’d prefer clear guidelines about what’s allowed and when we should disclose using it.

r001.rationale: The response describes teachers’ concern about whether AI supports learning or substitutes for understanding, but does not say their response stems from being unable to control students’ AI use.

sol-6.1.text: I think teachers are trying to figure out whether AI is helping students learn or just helping them finish homework. If a student submits an answer they can’t explain, it’s hard for the teacher to know what they actually understand. So I can understand the concern. But I also think there’s a difference between asking AI to explain something you’re stuck on and having it do the whole assignment. Clear rules about that distinction would help students use it responsibly.

r001.rationale: The response describes teachers’ concern about whether AI supports learning and whether students can explain submitted work. It does not say teachers are responding because they cannot control whether students use AI.
